prize_parts.citation: For showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, creating the theory of credit cycles.

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) provide a compact and original mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral values, together with the feedback between asset prices and credit, turn temporary shocks into persistent and amplified fluctuations. The idea is conceptually foundational and has been absorbed into macro-finance, quantitative macroeconomics and central-bank models. Its relevance after 2008 was clear, and almost three decades of follow-up give it strong maturity. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, with a two-author founding paper and no obvious missing originator. My opening ranking still stands after reading colleagues' arguments. The opening rankings show broad agreement that the mechanism is a core contribution, but I do not treat that as evidence of scientific merit. My reasons are the originality of the mechanism, its reach into theory, quantitative work and policy, and the clarity of credit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) may be read as having covered the neighbouring ground, and that direct empirical identification of the amplification magnitude is less clean than the theory. A second reservation is that limiting the award to Kiyotaki and Moore leaves the financial-accelerator strand (Gertler, Gilchrist) unrecognised, which some members consider part of the same achievement.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B002 first and adds Gertler, centring the award on collateral constraints while recognising the financial-accelerator strand. He accepts that Bernanke's 2022 prize and Gilchrist's claims limit the room for that strand.
responses.response: I agree that the strands are related and that the 2022 prize complicates the accelerator lineage. That complication is the reason I would keep the citation to two names. Adding Gertler would credit a different achievement, because the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator rests on agency costs in net worth and external finance premia rather than on collateral-asset price dynamics. It would also leave the attribution open to the objection that Bernanke, who is already a laureate, was the other originator of that strand. I would not treat Gertler's inclusion as disqualifying if the Committee prefers a broader citation. Under that option the citation should name the collateral-constraint mechanism first, and Gertler's case should be made on his own contribution, not on the support count.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B012 first and B002 third. He flags that overlap with the 2022 prize could reduce the Committee's appetite, and he confines B002 to Kiyotaki and Moore.
responses.response: I share his two-name attribution and I take the overlap concern seriously. My view is that the overlap is thematic and not a duplication of the discovery. The 2022 prize concerned the role of banks, runs and intermediation in crises. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how collateral values in the borrower's balance sheet create a dynamic feedback loop that propagates shocks over time. These are different mechanisms with different empirical implications. Committee practice treats the same field being revisited with a distinct discovery as acceptable, so I would not let the overlap decide the matter. I accept his point that, if the Committee judged the area saturated, B002 would be the one that loses.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B012 first. She argues that BLP demand estimation is both a method and a framework, with a compact three-person core and three decades of use in merger review, antitrust, trade and IO.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and reach. I ranked B012 fifth, not lower, because the toolkit has broad real-world impact. My reservation concerns the citation and attribution. The prize would reward a methodology whose credit is spread across Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, and also Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. Whether Pakes's dynamic-game work belongs in the same citation as the BLP demand-side core is unclear. If the Committee can write a crisp citation that does not exclude contributors whose work is foundational, I would raise B012 in my ordering. At present I think B002 has the cleaner credit and the more conceptual contribution, while recognising that the weight given to methods versus mechanisms is a real difference in judgment between us.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B021 first. She restricts the proposal to the Autor-Dorn-Hanson China-shock core, because the task framework has originators who are not on the credited list, and she regards the literature as mature enough to judge.
responses.response: I ranked B021 second and I agree with her restriction. On reflection I weigh the task-framework overlap with Acemoglu and Restrepo and with the Goldin-Katz skill-premium literature more heavily than I did in my opening, as Fredriksson's and Stromberg's openings also note. A China-shock citation is clean on attribution but the ongoing debate over persistence and magnitudes makes the long-run verdict less settled than for B002. Combining tasks and trade shocks risks an artificial bundle. For those reasons I keep B021 as an alternative and not as part of my preferred configuration. I would reconsider if the Committee judged the persistence evidence to be robust.

uncertainties: How much weight the Committee should give to the 2022 prize when judging the novelty of a second financial-frictions award.
Whether the accelerator strand (Gertler, Gilchrist) should be recognised alongside Kiyotaki and Moore or left out to keep the attribution clean.
Direct empirical identification of the size of collateral amplification, which is weaker than the theoretical case.

Whether a second part, for example Melitz on firm heterogeneity in trade, would strengthen the configuration or only add attribution problems, including the omission of Helpman and of credited contributors outside the three-person cap.
statement.conflict_note: I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell and a co-author of John Hassler, and an IIES colleague of both. Both rank B002 first and propose adding Gertler, which is not a recusal ground on its own but should be weighed. I have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (also with Aghion, Bergeaud and Li), a credited name on B017, which is not in my preferred configuration or alternatives. The profile shows no apparent connection to Kiyotaki, Moore, Melitz, Helpman, Autor, Dorn or Hanson. The profile gives weak evidence that I may have helped draft the 2025 Scientific Background, which does not bear on this slate.
